location: Nauvis - Crash Site - Starter Raw Coal Deposit
summary: The deposits here are abundant, but nothing about this planet is easy. Coal burns filthy and leaves ash everywhere, clogging machines almost as soon as they begin running. Copper refuses to cooperate unless I feed it water. Every step forward demands another layer of infrastructure. Nothing is simple extraction — everything is dependency.

Even the ground itself resists me. The soil on this planet isn’t suitable for proper construction. Structures sink, shift, or refuse placement unless I lay down a stone foundation first. Before I can build industry, I have to build the ground it stands on.

With only a single mining drill, progress feels painfully slow. The drill devours raw coal fast. Most of the day was spent breaking rocks and chopping trees just to keep the miner alive. It’s a brutal loop — mining fuel so the drill can mine materials so I can build more drills.

Somehow, I managed to produce enough iron to fabricate pipes and run water to the copper veins. That moment — watching water finally flow — felt like real progress. By nightfall I had miners running on coal, copper, and iron. Not efficiently. Not cleanly. But running.

When darkness fell, the creatures came. Giant insectoid things — relentless and angry. They attacked in waves. I held the line, but only barely. I built a few makeshift mini turrets and loaded them with wooden magazines. I even boxed them in with flimsy wooden fences — crude and probably flammable, but it made me feel like I was building a wall instead of just surviving. The turrets are weak and don’t hit very hard, but they fire consistently. For now, that’s enough.

The fighting never stopped once it began. I counted without meaning to: 64 level-one common biters, 6 level-one common spitters, 1 level-one acidic spitter, 1 level-one fast spitter, 1 level-one inferno spitter, 1 level-one spawner spitter, and 1 level-one wasp spitter.

Throughout the first night, I lost 8 flimsy wooden fences and burned through 19 wooden magazines just to keep the perimeter intact. The damage could have been worse, but the flimsy wooden fences were cheap and I replaced them before the Defense collapsed.

There were moments during the night where I nearly died. More than once I was forced to fight them by hand when ammunition ran low or a turret ran dry. Claws scraped across my armor. Acid hissed against metal. I could hear my own breathing inside the helmet, fast and uneven. I survived by inches.

Morning brought a fragile calm. The miners are running. The fences are patched. The attacks have eased, though they haven’t stopped entirely. I used the brief quiet to sketch out better miner placements and future layouts. If I’m going to survive here, I can’t just work harder. I have to work smarter.
